newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan ruling party in crisis after resignations.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan ruling party in crisis after resignations.

text.p: Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party, already under fire for the island's deteriorating social order, now faces a political crisis following the resignation of one of its most popular ministers.

Minister without portfolio Ma Ying-jeou dropped a bombshell on Thursday by offering his resignation to Premier Lien Chan, saying he had decided to quit because he was disappointed with the government failure's to deal with public discontent.
Interior Minister Lin Feng-cheng and Council of Agriculture chairman Tjiu Mau-ying also resigned, but neither matches Ma's superstar status.
Analysts said Ma's resignation would deal the heaviest blow to the Nationalist Party, whose image has been tainted by allegations of corruption and Taiwan's worsening social order.

"Ma is one of the few senior officials really loved by the public, and his resignation, seen as a silent protest, could fuel the public discontent toward the government," said Hu Fu, a politics professor at the National Taiwan University.
An opinion poll published on Friday by the local China Times showed that 81 percent of Taiwan people had been "impressed" by Ma's performance as an official.
"Ma was an image trump card of the party and his resignation would hurt both the party and the government seriously," a Nationalist official told Reuters.
In a strongly worded statement after his resignation, Ma, 47, criticised the political situation where officials "struggle for powers and credits and shun responsibility."

"I feel deeply ashamed for a series of recent incidents that have led to rapid falling of the public trust in the government," Ma, known as the "Golden Boy" of Taiwan's political circle, told a news conference.
His resignation came as anti-government sentiment erupted following a spate of violent crimes that have hit Taiwan since November.

The recent kidnap and murder of a famous actress's daughter, the gangland-style execution of a local government head and seven other people, and the rape and murder of an opposition feminist have brough the crime issue to a head.
More than 50,000 people protested in Taipei last Sunday against the government's failure to stop crime and demanded that Lien and his cabinet resign.
The protest prompted President Lee Teng-hui, who doubles as chairman of the ruling Nationalist Party, to call for a partial reshuffle of the cabinet on Wednesday.
Chiu Yi-jen, secretary-general of the main opposition Democratic Progressive Party, said the public could lose confidence in the government following Ma's resignation.
"Ma's move also represents worsening political ethics within the Nationalist Party, which has threatened internal stability and political reforms in Taiwan," he said.

"If the Nationalist Party wants to patch up its image and ease public discontent, the best way is to replace the premier and reshuffle the cabinet (as soon) as the public has desired," political science professor Chang Lin-cheng of National Taiwan University said.

"But again this is only shortlived because the basic problem lies with the the top leadership and the political system. Right now, the president has the power, but he is not checked by parliament. The premier who is responsible to parliament can only execute the president's policies."
"It is something the Nationalist Party should ponder and improve, if it is to retain its rulership in the future," she said.
Premier Lien tendered his resignation earlier in the week. Although President Lee declined to accept it, he asked Lien to propose changes in cabinet positions next week.
Ma's resignation also disrupted the ruling party's plan to have him challenge incumbent Taipei mayor Chen Shui-bian in the 1998 mayoral elections.
Ma had been widely regarded as the Nationalists' best hope of unseating Chen, a member of the main opposition Democratic Progressive Party, and regaining control of the capital.
